html:
Buganda is the kingdom of the Baganda people on the north shore of Lake Victoria, at the centre of modern Uganda. The map shows it from 1815 to 1900, when it was one of the strongest states in East Africa.

Tradition names Kato Kintu as its first king, the Kabaka, in about the 1300s. Buganda grew at the expense of its larger neighbour Bunyoro in the 1700s and 1800s.

In the 1840s Arab and Swahili traders reached the court. Kabaka Mutesa I welcomed British explorers and, in 1877 and 1879, Protestant and Catholic missionaries. Christians, Muslims and followers of the old religion became rival parties at court. His son Mwanga had many young converts put to death, the Uganda Martyrs of 1885 to 1887, and religious civil war followed.

Britain made Buganda the centre of its Uganda Protectorate in 1894, and the 1900 Buganda Agreement gave its chiefs large estates. The name Uganda itself comes from the Swahili word for Buganda. After independence the kingdom was abolished in 1967 and restored as a cultural monarchy in 1993.
